extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator — literate early-18th-century public interested in manners, theatre, music, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Curated Spectator essays (Addison & Steele) giving prescriptive guidelines and judgments about fame, ambition, theatre, music, salutations, and growing old — moral and aesthetic advice for the general reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining fame requires continuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be always a noble Train of Actions to preserve his Fame in Life and Motion. Admiration is a very short-liv'd Passion, that immediately decays upon growing familiar with its Object, unless it be still fed with fresh Discoveries, and kept alive by a new perpetual Succession of Miracles rising up to its View.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Do not rest on past achievements — reputation naturally flags if not continually renewed. Examples/notes: even extraordinary actions become expected from a celebrated person and may fail to enhance (and even diminish) reputation if they fall below high expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single deep blot outweighs many smaller merits
rubrics_metrics.description: If by a mistaken Pursuit after Fame, or through human Infirmity, any false Step be made in the more momentous Concerns of Life, the whole Scheme of ambitious Designs is broken and disappointed. The smaller Stains and Blemishes may die away amidst the Brightness ... but a Blot of a deeper Nature casts a Shade on all the other Beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring guidance: small slip/weaknesses are conspicuous and can be forgiven by great merit, but serious misdeeds or important false steps can destroy a reputation regardless of other virtues. Note: aggravation by rivals or former equals magnifies the damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame is a poor source of lasting happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame brings the ambitious Man very little Happiness, but subjects him to much Uneasiness and Dissatisfaction. It is an empty imaginary Good ... It may indeed fill the Mind for a while with a giddy kind of Pleasure, but it is such a Pleasure as makes a Man restless and uneasy under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: pursuing fame tends to inflame desire rather than satisfy it; the enjoyment is precarious and dependent on others. Examples: many who attain desired fame still thirst for more; praise can mortify if it falls short of expectation; silence or censure causes acute distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition produces inward turmoil and vulnerability to praise and reproach
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition raises a secret Tumult in the Soul, it inflames the Mind, and puts it into a violent Hurry of Thought ... If the ambitious Man can be so much grieved even with Praise itself, how will he be able to bear up under Scandal and Defamation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral criterion: an ambitious temperament makes one highly dependent on others' opinions; cultivate temperance or redirect ambition toward more stable ends to avoid mental disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seek the praise of created beings; proper judgment and reward come from the Supreme
rubrics_metrics.description: No other Being can make a right Judgment of us, and esteem us according to our Merits. Created Beings see nothing but our Outside ... the great Sovereign of the World beholds every Perfection in its Obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: it is folly to seek the praise of any being besides the Supreme, both because mortal judgment is limited/misleading and because created beings cannot confer the highest reward. Practical take: orient desire for fame toward divine approbation rather than human applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuing fame can hinder attainment of ultimate (spiritual) happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The strong Desire of Fame breeds several vicious Habits in the Mind. Many of those Actions which are apt to procure Fame are not in their Nature conducive to this our ultimate Happiness. If the same Actions were proper Instruments for both, they would nevertheless fail in the Attainment of this last End, if they proceeded from a Desire of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral check: assess whether actions taken to gain public esteem are compatible with deeper ends; motivation matters — identical acts produce different moral outcomes when motivated by vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage entertainments should both 'do' and 'say' (action and instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: All who go there should see something which may improve them in a Way of which they are capable. In short ... I would have something done as well as said on the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic guideline: theatre should offer both intellectual and physical/visual entertainment to suit different audiences. Example/antipattern: including physical acts (rope-dancers, tumblers) to appeal to 'corporeal Wits' is proposed as a way to broaden appeal; care should be taken to balance quality and popular accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music should heighten poetry and express passion; mere sounds are empty
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick only valuable, as it is agreeable to, and heightens the Purpose of Poetry ... meer musical Sounds are in our Art no other than nonsense Verses are in Poetry. Musick therefore must always have some Passion or Sentiment to express, or else Violins, Voices, or any other Organs of Sound, afford an Entertainment very little above the Rattles of Children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic standard: compositions (especially vocal/opera) must convey sentiment and serve the poetic text. Practical: align musical composition to poetic purpose; avoid pure display of sound detached from expressive meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for presenting musical entertainments
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals: make a Subscription of two Guineas, for eight Times; that the Entertainment, with the Names of the Authors of the Poetry, may be printed, to be sold in the House, with an Account of the several Authors of the Vocal as well as the Instrumental Musick for each Night; the Money to be paid at the Receipt of the Tickets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural guidance for producers: professionalize music presentation by printing programs with author/composer credits, using subscription funding, and making transparency of authorship part of the offering; stated cultural aim: 'reviving an Art' and establishing settled notions of music to counter 'Barbarism under an Affectation of Knowledge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Salutations must be governed by right reason and appropriateness of time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some Things which cannot come under certain Rules, but which one would think could not need them. Of this kind are outward Civilities and Salutations ... in the Royal Presence, I have often on publick Occasions thought it a very great Absurdity in the Company (during the Royal Presence) to exchange Salutations from all Parts of the Room, when certainly Common Sense should suggest, that all Regards at that Time should be engaged, and cannot be diverted to any other Object, without Disrespect to the Sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etiquette rule: avoid exchanging salutations during moments demanding collective attention (e.g., royal presence, parts of religious service). Be guided by 'common sense' (right reason) rather than mechanical custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and excess in civilities; be mindful of how refusals and over-obsequiousness read
rubrics_metrics.description: You shall sometimes see a Man begin the Offer of a Salutation, and observe a forbidding Air ... and stop short ... This in the Person ... is justly resented with a Coldness the whole ensuing Season. Others you shall find so obsequious, and so very courteous, as there is no escaping their Favours of this Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social guidance: intentionally withholding a salute ('preventing Aspect') breeds resentment; excessive obsequiousness or public demonstrations of civility can be insincere or inappropriate. Aim for moderation and genuine civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to worshippers and converts; public civility should not scandalize others
rubrics_metrics.description: A Dissenter of Rank ... feared he was not well-bred enough to be a Convert. ... It is worth considering whether, in regard to awkward People with scrupulous Consciences, a good Christian of the best Air in the World ought not rather to deny herself the Opportunity of shewing so many Graces, than keep a bashful Proselyte without the Pale of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious-context etiquette: curb outward pomp and conspicuous civility in worship spaces to avoid alienating or scandalizing prospective converts or those of other persuasions; sometimes forbearance is a charitable choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of growing old: prioritize durable, worthy actions over transient pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: You must propose, that no one set his Heart upon what is transient; the Beauty grows wrinkled while we are yet gazing at her. ... the Memory of good and worthy Actions is a Feast which must give a quicker Relish to the Soul than ever it could possibly taste in the highest Enjoyments or Jollities of Youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life-guidance: invest time and resources in generous, charitable, or public-spirited acts so that in old age one enjoys the lasting satisfaction of achievements rather than bitter memory of wasted pleasures. Practical admonition: reform early rather than expecting desires to vanish with age.
